assessment.rationale: Good as a wire-layer boundary specimen, weak as a full corrupt-chunk replication answer. Deterministic CBOR, pCID dispatch, and explicit unsupported/unverified handling fit local and no-central-authority goals, but chunk hash rejection, retry, and peer-local accounting are delegated to payload or wrapper protocols rather than specified here.
strengths: Deterministic CBOR and exact-byte canonicalization support reproducible audit of what was sent.
The minimal [pcid, payload] envelope keeps layer boundaries explicit and composes cleanly with external CAS or feed protocols.
Unknown pCIDs are handled locally and must be marked unsupported/unverified, avoiding silent trust and central registry assumptions.
weaknesses: The specimen does not define chunk-feed replication semantics, CID mismatch handling, retry policy, or peer-local accounting records.
The base envelope has no built-in signature or authorship field, so integrity and blame evidence depend on extra wrapper protocols.
The spec is still a draft with no freeze or minted spec pCID, so long-term interoperability is not yet demonstrated.
risks: Different implementations may expose unknown-pCID payload bytes differently, creating operator confusion around corrupt or unauthenticated content.
If wrapper signatures or CAS checks are omitted, Mallory's bad bytes may travel farther before rejection.
Clean wire-layer separation could be overrated here while replication and accounting rules remain underspecified.
open_questions: Which payload or wrapper protocol binds a feed entry to CID C and records local rejection when bytes do not match?
How are retry/backoff and peer-local reputation or accounting represented without central enforcement?
Should best-effort salvage from unknown pCIDs be further constrained when content is corrupt or unsigned?
assessment.authority_boundary: Evidence only; does not settle PromiseGrid design.
